summary: For ages 7–8, this is a REPRESENTATIONAL skill: fluently constructing AND interpreting life-cycle diagrams. Children place developmental stages in order, label them, draw directional transition arrows meaning 'develops/transforms into', and crucially close the loop with an arrow from the adult back to the egg/seed, because the adult produces new eggs or seeds. The diagram is a cycle, not a timeline with an end. Teaching compares the same diagram grammar across species (butterfly's 4-stage complete metamorphosis vs grasshopper's 3-stage incomplete vs flowering plant's seed→seedling→mature→flower→seed), moving from reading a finished diagram, to labelling a blank, to ordering jumbled stages, to constructing from scratch. Both producing and interpreting matter.
misconceptions: Drawing a life cycle as a straight LINE with a start and end, not a closed loop — missing that the adult produces the next generation.
Reversing or omitting arrows, so the 'develops into' direction is lost or ambiguous.
Assuming every animal's cycle has the same number of stages (forcing a pupa into a grasshopper, or expecting metamorphosis in a mammal).
Treating the diagram as a size/growth picture (small→big) rather than distinct developmental STAGES.
Confusing which stage is which — e.g. calling a caterpillar the 'baby butterfly' rather than the larva stage, or the pupa 'sleeping'.
Thinking the plant cycle has no 'reproduction' step because there's no obvious 'egg', missing that seed/flower play that role.

activities.title: Build and close a life-cycle ring
steps: Place stage pictures around a ring-shaped layout in the correct order — for a butterfly: egg, caterpillar (larva), chrysalis (pupa), adult butterfly.
Draw a transition arrow from each stage to the next, pointing in the 'develops into' direction.
Draw the final arrow from the adult back to the egg, so the ring closes (the adult lays eggs that begin the cycle again).
Say aloud what each arrow means — e.g. 'the caterpillar changes into a chrysalis over time'.
activities.insight: A life cycle is a closed loop with no end: the adult produces the next generation, and arrows mark changes that happen over time (each stage develops into the next, and the closing adult→egg arrow means the adult lays eggs), not just pointers to the next picture.

activities.title: Compare two cycles side by side
steps: Build or examine a butterfly ring (4 stages) next to a grasshopper ring (egg→nymph→adult, 3 stages).
Also compare a flowering plant cycle: seed→seedling→mature plant→flower/fruit→seed.
State at least one difference using both diagrams — e.g. 'the butterfly has a pupa/chrysalis stage; the grasshopper doesn't.'
Identify what plays the 'reproduction' role in the plant (seed/flower), since there is no obvious egg.
activities.insight: The same diagram grammar (nodes, directional arrows, closed loop) carries different content: different organisms have different numbers and kinds of stages, which is why you cannot force one template onto every organism.

activities.title: Read a finished cycle (interpret mode)
steps: Given a completed, labelled cycle (e.g. a butterfly or frog), answer a question that fits that organism, such as 'what comes right after the pupa?' (butterfly) or 'what comes right after the tadpole?' (frog), or 'what happens along this arrow?'
Point to any one arrow and explain what is happening between those two pictures.
Explain why the diagram comes back round to the start instead of stopping at the adult.
Name each stage correctly — e.g. caterpillar = larva, chrysalis = pupa — rather than 'baby butterfly' or 'sleeping'.
activities.insight: A diagram is a tool to think WITH: you should be able to extract order, transitions and meaning from someone else's diagram, not only produce your own.

activities.title: Freehand transfer on paper
steps: Given a list of an organism's stages, draw your own labelled cycle on paper from scratch.
Add an arrowhead to every arrow to show direction, and close the loop back to the start.
Choose the correct number of stages for the organism (don't copy the butterfly's four onto a bird or grasshopper).
Label each stage with its proper name.
activities.insight: You own the conventions when you can produce a correct, looped, labelled diagram unaided, with the shape matching the organism's real life cycle.

checkQuestion: Here is a frog's life cycle drawn as a ring of pictures joined by arrows. Point to any one arrow and tell me what it means — what is happening between those two pictures? Then, using this list of butterfly stages, draw your own diagram that shows the same kind of loop.
checkAnswer: An arrow means 'changes into / grows into over time' — it marks a transition from one stage to the next. The diagram is a closed ring because the adult produces young that begin the cycle again. The child draws egg → caterpillar (larva) → chrysalis (pupa) → butterfly → (lays eggs), with arrows closing the loop back to the egg.
